title: How Data Center AI Can Keep Growing, Despite Supply Chain Bottlenecks
gist: Geoff Tate argues data center AI keeps compounding through foundry, memory, power and laser shortages because the biggest buyers (Nvidia, Google, Amazon, Anthropic, OpenAI) already locked in supply, cheaper models and SLMs cut demand per task, and new architectures (TPU/Trainium, Google's Frozen v2 Gemini-in-silicon, SRAM-heavy Groq/Cerebras designs, optical compute) squeeze more tokens per watt and per wafer. His investor punchline is what happens when supply catches up around 2028-2030: 'fortress' names at 18-36x earnings survive, while custom-silicon agents (Broadcom, Marvell at ~60x), laser makers (Coherent, Lumentum at >100x) and unprofitable neoclouds face commoditization and price crashes unless they build differentiated, sticky products.

insights.claim: The binding constraints on data center AI growth are foundry capacity, memory, power, and lasers rather than end demand, with the author framing efficiency as the number one coping strategy for the next two to five years.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Model AI growth as a supply-allocation problem: winners are whoever converts scarce wafers, HBM, MW and InP into tokens most efficiently.
insights.quote: The number one strategy for coping with supply chain bottlenecks is efficiency — get the most results out of what you have and what you can get.
insights.locator: The number one strategy for coping

insights.claim: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on the July 30th earnings call that AI demand is strong into 2028 and that revenue growth will eventually outpace incremental CapEx growth, making ROIC compelling a few years out.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Jassy is pre-framing the payback debate: watch the CapEx-to-revenue growth crossover as the key sentiment trigger for hyperscaler multiples.
insights.quote: as we get a few years out and the revenue growth outpaces the incremental CapEx growth, which will happen at some point, the resulting revenue, free cash flow, and return on invested capital is very compelling.
insights.locator: On Amazon’s July 30th earnings call

insights.claim: All major hyperscalers recently raised CapEx plans partly because of rising input costs, not purely because of added capacity, meaning headline CapEx increases overstate the real compute being added.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Deflate reported CapEx growth by input-cost inflation before inferring unit compute growth; cost-push CapEx compresses returns.
insights.quote: Recently, all the major hyperscalers announced earnings and increased CapEx plans (partly due to rising costs).
insights.locator: Recently, all the major hyperscalers

insights.claim: Supply chain access has followed a Gold Rush dynamic in which first movers with the most capital and best supply chain management, such as Nvidia and Google, have already locked in most of the capacity they need.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Late entrants cannot buy their way in at any price; the scarcity premium accrues to incumbents with pre-existing allocations.
insights.quote: Like the Gold Rush, those who moved first and fastest seized the most and best supply capacity.
insights.locator: Like the Gold Rush, those who moved

insights.claim: Companies whose models failed to generate demand are monetizing stranded compute: after SpaceX merged with xAI, the combined entity signed a $45 billion deal with Anthropic for access to 220K Nvidia GPUs and 300MW ahead of its IPO.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: A compute resale market is forming; watch it as a pressure valve that lets model labs scale without their own CapEx, and as a signal of who over-built.
insights.quote: A $45 billion deal with Anthropic, giving them access to 220K Nvidia GPUs and 300MW;
insights.locator: SpaceX merged with xAI

insights.claim: The SpaceX/xAI excess-capacity deals also include a $920 million per month arrangement with Google through mid-2029 for roughly 110K GPUs and a $6.3 billion Reflection AI deal for Nvidia GB300 chips.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Roughly $8.4/GPU-hour-equivalent economics for rented frontier capacity set a market clearing price other neocloud contracts will be benchmarked against.
insights.quote: A $920 million/month deal with Google through mid-2029 for ~110K GPUs, and
insights.locator: A $920 million/month deal with Google

insights.claim: Meta announced it will sell or rent excess AI computing power, including a potential $10 billion deal with Anthropic, turning a hyperscaler's own buildout into a merchant capacity business.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: If first-party buyers start reselling, it caps how tight the rental market can get and directly threatens neocloud pricing power.
insights.quote: Meta recently announced it will sell/rent excess AI computing power, including a potential $10 billion deal with Anthropic.
insights.locator: Meta recently announced it will sell/rent

themes.theme: Model-tier arbitrage and the China token share

insights.claim: Frontier model pricing spans a ~30x range — GPT-5.5 at $30/million tokens, GPT-5.4 at $15/million, and DeepSeek V4 at under $1/million per OpenRouter — so routing tasks to the cheapest adequate model is the single largest lever on inference cost.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Price compression at the low end means token volume growth will not translate into proportional frontier-lab revenue; watch blended revenue per token.
insights.quote: For example, GPT-5.5 costs $30/million tokens; GPT-5.4 is half that at $15/million tokens. DeepSeek V4 is less than $1/million tokens.
insights.locator: The best frontier models have immense capability

insights.claim: Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong said in June that the company cut internal AI spending nearly in half simply by defaulting its engineers to open Chinese models (Zhipu AI GLM 5.2 and Moonshot AI Kimi K2.7).
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Enterprise switching costs between models are near zero at the default-config level — a direct margin threat to US frontier API revenue.
insights.quote: cut its internal AI spending nearly in half by setting the default model for its engineers to open models from China
insights.locator: Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong revealed on X

insights.claim: Chinese models occupied 8 of the top 10 slots by tokens used on OpenRouter's leaderboard as of late July, with only Nvidia's Nemotron 3 and Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8 breaking through.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Token-share, not revenue-share, is where Chinese open models have already won; that is a leading indicator of Western API price erosion.
insights.quote: OpenRouter’s LLM Leaderboard, as of late July, had Chinese models as 8 of the top 10 by tokens used
insights.locator: OpenRouter, valued recently at $1.3 billion

insights.claim: Investment firm William Blair estimates Chinese models accounted for 30% of tokens used by U.S. firms since February, a penetration level that is a geopolitical and commercial exposure most US AI bulls do not price in.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Any policy ban on Chinese open weights would abruptly re-price US inference demand upward; the reverse is a persistent deflationary drag.
insights.quote: Chinese models accounted for 30% of tokens used by U.S. firms since February, according to investment firm William Blair.
insights.locator: Chinese models accounted for 30%

insights.claim: OpenRouter, valued at $1.3 billion, is positioned as the buy-versus-build answer to model routing, letting enterprises capture cheap-model arbitrage without writing their own router.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Routing/aggregation layers capture value from model commoditization — a structurally long position on price competition among labs.
insights.quote: OpenRouter, valued recently at $1.3 billion, provides a unified interface for a wide range of LLMs.
insights.locator: OpenRouter, valued recently at $1.3 billion

insights.claim: Thinking Machines, led by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, shipped a first model with nearly 1 trillion parameters but only 41 billion active, explicitly optimizing cost-performance over raw power, plus a fine-tuning tool called Tinker.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Sparse-activation architectures decouple capability from serving cost — the key mechanism that lets inference demand grow without proportional GPU demand.
insights.quote: The model has nearly 1 trillion parameters, but only 41 billion are “active,” so only a fraction of the model is used to deal with any query.
insights.locator: Thinking Machines, run by former OpenAI

insights.claim: Small language models trained only on a narrow task set (e.g., a bilingual English/Spanish virtual assistant) can be small enough to run on a local server or future consumer hardware, with a Mac Studio with M7 Ultra expected in 2028 to support models above 1 trillion parameters.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: On-device and on-prem inference caps the addressable data-center token pool for high-volume repetitive workloads — a long-dated headwind for cloud inference capacity.
insights.quote: Mac Studio with M7 Ultra in 2028 is expected to support models with more than 1 trillion parameters
insights.locator: An SLM might even be small enough

insights.claim: SemiAnalysis reports Anthropic's annualized revenue run rate per megawatt rose 4x in just nine months, evidence that frontier labs are extracting far more revenue per unit of scarce power.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Revenue per MW is the cleanest efficiency KPI in a power-constrained regime; 4x in 9 months means power scarcity binds later than headline forecasts assume.
insights.quote: SemiAnalysis reports that Anthropic’s ARR (annualized revenue run rate) per MW (megawatt) is 4x higher in just 9 months.
insights.locator: Frontier model companies are substantially increasing

insights.claim: Allstate described in December that its virtual assistants handle 4 of 10 customer calls, freeing salaried staff — a concrete enterprise ROI datapoint on modest AI spend.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Deflection rates near 40% in a regulated insurer are the kind of proof point that sustains enterprise AI budgets through a CapEx scare.
insights.quote: Allstate in December described how its virtual assistants are able to handle 4 of 10 customer calls, freeing up salaried staff.
insights.locator: Customer usage of AI is growing

insights.claim: Agentic AI increases the benefit per task but consumes many more tokens, so agentic adoption is the demand-side force that offsets per-token efficiency gains.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Token volume and token price move in opposite directions; net inference revenue depends on which curve wins — track tokens/task, not just tokens.
insights.quote: Agentic AI brings more benefits, but uses many more tokens.
insights.locator: Customer usage of AI is growing

themes.theme: Silicon architecture divergence away from general-purpose GPUs

insights.claim: Nvidia paid $20 billion to license Groq's technology and Cerebras went public at a $42 billion market cap, both validating HBM-free, SRAM-heavy architectures for the highest-responsiveness leading-edge inference workloads.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: SRAM-centric inference silicon is a partial hedge against the HBM bottleneck — a structural reason HBM demand may not scale linearly with inference.
insights.quote: Nvidia paid $20 billion to license Groq’s technology, and Cerebras has gone public ($42 billion market cap as of late July) because it developed architectures without HBM, but with lots of SRAM
insights.locator: GPUs are general-purpose and optimized

insights.claim: Amazon said on its recent earnings call that Trainium's revenue run rate exceeds $25 billion per year, and claims better throughput per dollar and per watt on internal workloads than merchant silicon.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: A $25B+ internal accelerator line is now large enough to materially dent Nvidia's incremental TAM; watch external Trainium sales to Anthropic and OpenAI.
insights.quote: Amazon, on its recent earnings call, said Trainium’s revenue run rate exceeds $25 billion/year.
insights.locator: Google has been developing TPUs for a decade

insights.claim: Both Google and Amazon are moving from internal-only custom silicon to selling it externally — Google with Anthropic and Meta deals plus neocloud talks, Amazon with Anthropic and OpenAI deals.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler silicon becoming merchant silicon converts captive volume into direct competition for Nvidia and AMD at the rack level.
insights.locator: Both are now selling or planning to sell

insights.claim: Google's Frozen v2 chip hard-codes parts of the Gemini model into silicon, targets release as early as 2028, and aims for 6x to 10x more tokens per watt than current hardware — which also stretches Google's limited TSMC wafer allocation.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Model-specific ASICs are the endgame of efficiency; if 6-10x tokens/W lands, per-token cost floors collapse for whoever controls both model and silicon.
insights.quote: The goal is to process 6x to 10x more tokens per watt than current hardware
insights.locator: Google is developing a chip, code-named Frozen v2

insights.claim: OpenAI is building its own accelerator with Broadcom and Anthropic is rumored to be exploring its own chip, meaning the owners of the most-used frontier models will co-optimize silicon to their model architectures.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Vertical integration by the labs is the biggest medium-term risk to merchant GPU share and to custom-silicon vendors' bargaining power.
insights.locator: OpenAI is developing its own AI accelerator

insights.claim: The big players' in-house CPUs (Nvidia Vera, Amazon Graviton and others) are claimed to be 20% to 50% more efficient than x86 CPUs, and Nvidia's Vera CPU is specifically optimized for agentic AI.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: A 20-50% efficiency edge in data center CPUs is an ongoing share transfer away from x86 incumbents inside the highest-growth segment.
insights.quote: which are claimed to be 20% to 50% more efficient than x86 CPUs
insights.locator: The big players are developing their own CPUs

insights.claim: A long tail of accelerator startups — FuriosaAI, Nuvacore, D-Matrix, Etched (claiming $1 billion of pre-orders), Tenstorrent, Sambanova, Mat-X, Positron, Majestic Labs — face a wafer-allocation ceiling on success, making acquisition by a capacity-rich player the likeliest exit.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Wafer allocation, not product-market fit, is the gating factor for AI chip startups — price M&A optionality rather than standalone scaling.
insights.quote: They might have a hard time getting wafer allocations if they get traction, but they could be acquired by a big player with capacity.
insights.locator: There are numerous startups developing architectural

insights.claim: Neurophos in Austin claims an optical structure integrated on a CMOS process at an unnamed foundry will deliver up to 250x the AI compute performance of Nvidia Blackwell 200, a claim the author flags as unverified pending real systems.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Optical compute is the highest-variance disruption to the GPU stack; treat the 250x claim as a watch item, not a forecast.
insights.quote: Neurophos claims it will soon deliver superior AI compute performance, up to 250x that of Nvidia Blackwell 200
insights.locator: Coming soon is optical compute from Neurophos

insights.claim: Early optical compute companies failed because the cost and time of digital-to-optical-and-back conversion exceeded the optical speed benefit, so UK-based Lumai's lens-based matrix-multiply approach only works if it keeps a large enough block of continuous compute in the optical domain.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: This conversion-overhead test is the right screen for evaluating any optical compute pitch — apply it before underwriting the category.
insights.quote: Early optical compute companies failed because the cost and time to convert from the digital domain to optical, then back, exceeded the benefit of the optical speed.
insights.locator: Another optical compute company, Lumai

themes.theme: Who is swimming naked when supply catches up

insights.claim: The author predicts data center AI supply will catch up with demand sometime around 2028 to 2030, ending the windfall-profit regime for anyone holding compute, memory, power, or lasers.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Set a 2028-2030 planning horizon for shortage-driven margins; contracts and backlogs extending past that window are the ones worth paying for.
insights.quote: But eventually (2028? 2029? 2030?), supply will catch up with demand for data center AI.
insights.locator: Everyone that has data center AI compute

insights.claim: The author's 'fortress' list of durable AI franchises is Anthropic, OpenAI and Google Gemini in models; Google, Amazon and Microsoft in hyperscale; Nvidia and AMD in GPUs; and TSMC in foundry — all of which trade at P/E ratios of 18 to 36 except AMD.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: A concentrated quality screen for AI exposure: 18-36x earnings for franchises with locked-in supply is the author's implied value case.
insights.quote: Except for AMD, these “fortress” companies have P/E ratios of 18 to 36, which are consistent with their expected rapid earnings growth.
insights.locator: These companies have strong franchises

insights.claim: AMD trades at a P/E well over 100 purely because investors expect significant GPU share gains over the next few years, making it the highest-expectations name in the fortress group.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: AMD is the pure expectations trade in AI compute: any stall in GPU share gains de-rates a >100x multiple hard.
insights.quote: AMD has a much higher P/E ratio, well over 100, because investors expect they’ll grow their GPU share significantly over the next few years.
insights.locator: AMD has a much higher P/E ratio

insights.claim: Broadcom and Marvell trade near 60x earnings but are structurally agents of hyperscalers that own the cloud, the models, and the accelerator architecture, and face growing commoditization risk as customers add alternatives like MediaTek.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: The custom-silicon bull case rests on customer concentration that is actively eroding — 60x multiples on agency businesses are the vulnerable link.
insights.quote: there is a growing risk of commoditization as the main players have increasing vendor choice
insights.locator: The leading AI custom silicon providers

insights.claim: The author expects hyperscalers to move downstream from architecture and design into silicon implementation over time, potentially acquiring smaller custom silicon providers and disintermediating Broadcom and Marvell.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Watch for hyperscaler acquisitions of ASIC design houses as the confirming signal to exit custom-silicon agency names.
insights.quote: over time, it seems likely the hyperscalers will move downstream from architecture/design to silicon implementation, perhaps acquiring some of the smaller custom silicon providers
insights.locator: So far, these hyperscalers have gone with

themes.theme: Memory and optics: escaping the commodity cycle

insights.claim: DRAM makers Micron, SK hynix and Samsung saw 10x stock price increases with multi-year backlogs, and SK hynix made more profit last quarter than in the previous five years combined, yet they still trade around 20x earnings because of historical boom-bust discounting.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: The ~20x multiple on record DRAM earnings is the market pricing peak-cycle earnings; the debate is whether custom HBM breaks the cycle.
insights.quote: SK hynix made more profit last quarter than in the last five years.
insights.locator: The stock market recently has seen 10x price increases

insights.claim: The thesis for permanently re-rating DRAM is customized HBM tuned to each AI accelerator architecture, which would require a business model shift from JEDEC commodity standards to custom ASIC engagements.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Watch for HBM contracts structured as custom ASIC design wins — that is the observable proof that DRAM has escaped commodity economics.
insights.quote: This requires a business model shift from JEDEC commodity to custom ASIC.
insights.locator: The DRAM companies may be able to get out

insights.claim: Laser makers Coherent and Lumentum have seen 10x stock surges and trade well above 100x earnings on the copper-to-optical interconnect shift, with Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston saying on CNBC the company is sold out for the next 5 years.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Five-year sold-out backlogs justify the multiple only if differentiation holds; the interconnect shift moves from scale-out to scale-up next.
insights.quote: We are sold out for the next 5 years.
insights.locator: Laser companies (Coherent, Lumentum) also have seen

insights.claim: InP laser fabrication is far less costly and complex than 2nm ASICs or HBM and has multiple other manufacturers, so Coherent and Lumentum risk a commodity price crash in two to five years unless they differentiate or acquire adjacent businesses like Optical Circuit Switches.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Low barriers to entry make optics the weakest moat in the AI supply chain despite the strongest current backlog — the clearest short-candidate framing in the piece.
insights.quote: the cost and complexity of the fabrication process is much less than 2nm ASICs or HBM
insights.locator: Both companies are trading at P/E ratios

insights.claim: Neoclouds such as CoreWeave and Nebius carry large valuations while unprofitable, and their core risk when supply exceeds demand is that hyperscalers will prioritize their own installed capacity over renting third-party compute.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Neocloud contract renewal rates post-2028 are the specific thing to monitor; they are the most levered losers of supply normalization.
insights.quote: The risk for the neoclouds, when supply exceeds demand, is that the major hyperscalers will have installed huge amounts of their own capacity and will prioritize that over renting from the neoclouds.
insights.locator: Finally, the neoclouds, such as Coreweave

insights.claim: The closing prescription is that windfall beneficiaries of the shortage must build differentiated and sticky offerings before supply normalizes, or face price crashes when commodity products go into oversupply.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Screen AI supply-chain holdings on differentiation and stickiness, not on current backlog length — backlog is the trap, not the moat.
insights.quote: Otherwise, they face price crashes when commodity products are in oversupply.
insights.locator: Players enjoying huge windfall profits
